accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS ELA W.4.7, W.4.8, W.5.7 and W.5.8: short research projects that investigate different aspects of a topic, relevant information from print and digital sources, taking notes, categorizing information and a list of sources; grade 5 adds summarize or paraphrase. The England KS2 equivalent (retrieve, record and present information from non-fiction) is named. Volcano facts used in the lab notes (most volcanoes form at plate boundaries, magma, eruptions) (most active volcanoes ring the Pacific, magma becomes lava at the surface, Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano) match USGS Volcano Hazards Program statements.

misconceptions.evidence: Wrong options target slips teachers see in grade 4–5 projects: a whole-topic question ('tell me everything'), an opinion question ('coolest'), trusting the first page found, believing the number of hits or any book beats any website, copying a whole sentence, changing 'most' into 'all' while shortening, citing 'the internet' or Google, and dropping the source list because notes are in own words.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagproj is a research-workflow lab: a question planner that refuses opinion, yes/no, whole-topic and repeated questions, a print/digital source sorter with an unreliable bin, a note picker that compares the copy and the meaning-changing note with the key-word paraphrase, a category filer and a two-source cross-check board. No other flag lab uses this mechanism and the 30 percent shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the child do the research move rather than read about it: they build three distinct questions, sort seven sources by format and trust, choose and justify a note, file six notes under their own question headings and resolve a disagreement by fetching a third source. Every wrong move prints a message naming the exact problem, such as 'That changes the fact'.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong answers: 'Yes, it covers it all' for a whole-topic question, 'Yes, books are always right' for print versus web, and 'The whole sentence copied out' for the best note. The task straight after each prediction disproves the wrong choice and the done message says whether the guess held.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with tagged wrong answers, each with its own message: 'the internet' as a source, no source list for paraphrased facts, an unnamed and undated post, a made-up story used for facts, a copied sentence, and a changed fact. Correct answers restate the rule in one line so the feedback teaches rather than only marks.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs score about grade 2.6 on validate_lessons with short sentences and one worked volcano example each; the adult text is about grade 7.7 and uses the exact standard terms research question, aspect, print source, digital source, reliable source, paraphrase, summarize, categorize, cross-check and list of sources.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed and explanation overlap with every other lesson is under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph covers one stage of the project (questions, sources, notes, sorting and checking) and the adult paragraphs cover standards, terms, named mistakes and what the lab asks, with no padding.

mobile.evidence: walk.cjs ran the whole lab on an iPhone 13 viewport as well as desktop: Show me completed every task, the challenge rendered, and buttons wrapped under the canvas without overflow. Source and note cards are full-width tap targets with tap-then-tap alternatives to dragging, so the lab works one-handed on a phone.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs found no axe WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme on desktop or iPhone and no console errors. Every canvas action has a labelled button, feedback goes to an aria-live status line, and the canvas aria-label reads the current questions, sorted sources and notes.

sources: Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, Writing W.4.7, W.4.8, W.5.7, W.5.8 (Research to Build and Present Knowledge)
